newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FORECAST-Philippine Dec inflation seen at 4.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Philippine Dec inflation seen at 4.9 pct.

text.p: Year-on-year inflation in the Philippines is seen rising to 4.9 percent in December from 4.5 percent in November, according to a Reuters poll of five analysts.
This would bring the 1996 full-year inflation average to 8.5 percent from 1995's 8.1 percent, they said.
The analysts' projections are in line with the Philippine Central Bank's full-year forecast of around 8.5 percent and near the upper limit of the government's target range of 7.5 to 8.7 percent.
The government is expected to announce the December and full-year inflation figures on January 6.
In the same poll, economists said inflation is projected to be even lower next year at 6.5 percent, in line with a government target.

The estimate for December was lower than earlier projections of 6.0 to 6.5 percent. Analysts said the figures were revised after the government announced lower-than-expected inflation in November because of lower rice prices.
"The November inflation was extremely low," said Cecilia Tanchoco, an economist at the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI).
The December projections take into account the impact of Christmas spending and the delayed effects of an oil price hike implemented earlier in the month, analysts said.

The government's Energy Regulatory Board raised the prices of petroleum products by an average of 79.75 centavos per litre on December 4, of which 50 centavos were passed on to consumers and the remaining 29.75 centavos were absorbed by a government-run oil buffer fund.
Nevertheless, "prices have been very stable. The oil price hikes did not have much of an inflationary impact," said Manuel Ghoseco, an economist with the Dharmala Securities brokerage.
He said the liberalised economic environment cushioned the negative effects of an oil price hike because of the unrestricted import of refined petroluem products.
"Eventually, we'll be aligning ourselves with the worldwide inflation rate of 4.0 to 5.0 percent," he added.
"The government's inflation target of 6.5 percent for next year is reasonable," said Conrad Andres, research head of DBP-Daiwa Securities.

Analysts said the two-percentage-point cut in banks' reserve requirements and an expected government budget surplus as a result of the passage of an important tax reform law would send interest rates lower in 1997.
This would bring down the cost of doing business in the country and pull down inflation further, they said.
All Asia Capital and Trust Corp said lending rates could go down to 12.2 percent in 1997 from the estimated 14.4 percent in 1996.
But the country's widening trade deficit and the clamour for higher wages could weaken the peso and hold back the declining trend in inflation, economists said.
However, an expected record $4.0 billion balance of payments surplus at the end of 1996 could help cover up the trade deficit and keep the peso stable, other analysts said.
"The trade deficit is part of our growth. We can't do without capital investments," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist at Metrobank.
Analysts had earlier said the trade deficit could widen to $13.5 billion to $14.0 billion in 1997 from the $12.0 billion-estimate in 1996.
Following were the inflation forecasts made by five institutions (in percentage terms):
Dec '96 Avg 1996 Avg 1997
All AsiaCapital 5.2 8.5 6.5
DBP-Daiwa Securities 4.7-4.9 8.4-8.6 6.5-7.0
Dharmala Securities 4.8-5.3 8.4 6.0-6.5
Metrobank 5.0 8.5 6.5
